title: Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, Perplexity & the AI Tool Landscape
subtitle: Compare the major AI tools, choose the right one for each task, and build a personal AI stack that is fast, affordable and safe
description:
There is no single "best" AI tool. Professionals who get the most from AI know which tool fits which job, and why. This intermediate course maps the landscape beyond a single assistant: **Google Gemini** and its Workspace integration, long context and multimodal skills; **Microsoft Copilot** inside Microsoft 365 and the governance it demands; **Perplexity** as a cited answer engine for research; **open-weight models** and running AI locally; image generators; and voice and video tools such as ElevenLabs and HeyGen.

You will learn a repeatable method for comparing outputs side by side, weigh cost, privacy and lock-in trade-offs, and finish by designing your own personal AI stack. The course is vendor-neutral and focuses on durable concepts, with clear notes wherever features vary by plan or region.
outcomes: Map AI tools into categories and explain what each category is best at
Use Gemini with Google Workspace and its long-context, multimodal capabilities for real tasks
Explain how Microsoft 365 Copilot uses work data and the permissions governance it requires
Run cited research in Perplexity and verify sources systematically
Explain open-weight models and the trade-offs of running AI locally
Choose image, voice and video tools responsibly, with consent and disclosure
Compare tools with a fair test and design a personal AI stack balancing cost, privacy and quality

lessons.title: Mapping the AI tool landscape
lessons.body:
### Why a map beats a leaderboard

Every few weeks a new model tops a benchmark or a new app goes viral. Chasing each one wastes time. A better approach is a **map**: categories of tools, what each category is good at, and which tool in each category fits your work. Individual products change quickly; the categories are far more stable.

### The seven categories

**1. General-purpose assistants.** Chat-based assistants such as Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and Microsoft Copilot. They write, analyse, reason, code, read files and images, and increasingly search the web and take actions. Most professionals need one primary assistant and benefit from access to a second for comparison.

**2. Embedded work copilots.** AI built into the tools you already use: Gemini inside Google Workspace, Microsoft 365 Copilot inside Word, Excel, Outlook and Teams, and AI features inside CRMs, design tools and project managers. Their superpower is **context**: they can work with your emails, files and meetings (within your permissions) without copy-pasting.

**3. Answer and research engines.** Tools such as Perplexity that are designed around search: every answer comes with citations, and follow-up questions refine the research. Many general assistants now include search and deep research modes too, so the line is blurring.

**4. Open-weight and local models.** Model families whose weights are published for download, such as Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek and Gemma. They can be run on your own hardware or private cloud, which offers control and privacy, at the cost of setup effort and usually some capability compared with the very best hosted models.

**5. Image generators.** Tools such as Midjourney, Google's Imagen, OpenAI's image generation and Adobe Firefly. They create and edit images from text and reference images.

**6. Voice and video tools.** Text-to-speech, voice cloning, dubbing and avatar video tools such as ElevenLabs and HeyGen, plus video generation models.

**7. Automation and agent platforms.** Tools that connect AI to workflows: automation platforms, agent builders and developer frameworks, often using standards such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect to other software.

### How the categories overlap

Assistants increasingly bundle search, image generation, voice and agents. That's convenient, but a bundled feature isn't always the strongest option for a specialised need. A creator producing weekly dubbed videos may still prefer a dedicated voice tool; a researcher may still prefer an answer engine's citation-first design. The map helps you notice when a specialist is worth it.

### Worked example: one campaign, many tools

A small agency in Dubai plans a product launch for a skincare client:

- **Research:** an answer engine to gather cited information on the market and advertising rules, verified by a team member.
- **Strategy and copy:** a general assistant to draft the strategy, captions and scripts from the brief.
- **Team documents:** the embedded copilot in their office suite to summarise client email threads and meeting notes.
- **Visuals:** an image tool for concept boards; real product photography for ads.
- **Voice-over:** a voice tool to produce Arabic and English narration from approved scripts, using a licensed stock voice.
- **Governance:** everything client-confidential stays inside tools covered by the agency's business agreements.

Nobody needed "the best AI". They needed the right tool per step.

### Sample output: your first map

A useful personal map is a simple table: Category | Tool I use | What I use it for | Plan/account | Data allowed. For example: "General assistant | [Tool] | drafting, analysis | Business plan | internal and confidential (minimised)". If a row is blank, you've found either a gap or a category you don't need.

### Pitfalls

- Switching tools every week and never building skill in any.
- Paying for five overlapping subscriptions.
- Using a consumer app for client data because it was the quickest to open.
- Assuming a tool's bundled feature is best-in-class.

### Availability note

Features, model names, prices and regional availability change frequently. This course names products to make examples concrete, but always confirm current capabilities in each vendor's official help centre.

First, general assistants like Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and Copilot: your all-rounders for writing, analysis and reasoning. Second, embedded copilots: AI inside the tools you already use, like your email, documents and spreadsheets. Their superpower is context. Third, answer engines like Perplexity, built around search with citations. Fourth, open-weight models like Llama, Mistral and Qwen, which you can run on your own hardware for more control. Fifth, image generators. Sixth, voice and video tools like ElevenLabs and HeyGen. And seventh, automation and agent platforms that connect AI to your workflows. Now, the categories overlap. Many assistants bundle search, images and voice. That's convenient, but for heavy, specialised work, a dedicated tool can still be worth it. Here's your exercise. Draw a simple table: category, the tool you use, what you use it for, which plan you're on, and what data you're allowed to put into it. That last column is the one most people forget, and it's the one that keeps you and your clients safe. Products change fast. Categories don't. Learn the map, and every new tool becomes easy to place.

keyTakeaways: Think in categories: assistants, embedded copilots, answer engines, open-weight models, image, voice/video, and automation.
Embedded copilots win on context; answer engines on citations; open-weight models on control.
Bundled features are convenient, but specialists can be worth it for heavy, specific needs.
Map your tools by use, plan and allowed data to find gaps and overlaps.

lessons.title: How to evaluate any AI tool in 30 minutes
lessons.body:
### The problem with hype

Demos show a tool at its best, on tasks chosen by the vendor. You need to know how it performs on **your** tasks, with **your** data rules, at **your** budget. A short, structured evaluation beats weeks of casual poking.

### The eight evaluation criteria

1. **Task fit:** does it do the job you need, not just impressive adjacent jobs?
2. **Output quality:** accuracy, relevance, tone, structure, on your real examples.
3. **Grounding and citations:** can it show where information comes from?
4. **Context and integration:** does it connect to where your work lives (documents, email, CRM), and can it handle your file sizes?
5. **Privacy and data terms:** is your data used for training? What retention and admin controls exist? Is there a business agreement?
6. **Cost:** subscription or usage price, limits, and cost per useful output.
7. **Reliability and support:** uptime, usage caps at busy times, help resources.
8. **Lock-in and portability:** can you export your prompts, files and outputs if you leave?

### The 30-minute evaluation sprint

**Minutes 0 to 5: Define three test tasks** from real work, ideally one easy, one typical and one hard. For a marketer: rewrite a product description; summarise a 20-page report; build a campaign plan with budget constraints.

**Minutes 5 to 20: Run the same prompts** in the tool you're evaluating and in your current tool. Use identical wording and the same attached materials (non-confidential).

```text
[Paste identical prompt]
Context: [same]
Materials: [same attachments]
Output format: [same]
```

**Minutes 20 to 25: Score blind if possible.** Paste outputs into a document labelled A and B without tool names, and score each 1 to 5 on accuracy, usefulness and effort-to-fix.

**Minutes 25 to 30: Check the non-output criteria.** Read the vendor's privacy page and plan comparison. Note limits and price.

### A simple scorecard

| Criterion | Tool A | Tool B | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Task 1 quality (1-5) | | | |
| Task 2 quality (1-5) | | | |
| Task 3 quality (1-5) | | | |
| Citations/grounding | | | |
| Integration fit | | | |
| Data terms suitable for our data? | | | |
| Monthly cost | | | |
| Export/portability | | | |

### Worked example

A sales team lead in Riyadh evaluates whether to add an answer engine alongside the team's general assistant. Test tasks: research a prospect company's recent news, summarise an industry regulation change, and draft a call plan. Results: the answer engine is faster and better cited on the two research tasks; the assistant is better at the call plan. Decision: keep the assistant as primary, add the answer engine for a two-week trial with three reps, and review.

### Sample judgement notes

Useful notes are specific: "Tool B's summary missed the exemption in section 4; Tool A caught it and quoted it." "Tool A cited a 2023 article for a current fee; Tool B linked to the regulator's page." Specific notes make decisions defensible and help colleagues reproduce your test.

### Fairness rules for comparisons

- Same prompt, same materials, same time.
- Test more than once for important decisions; outputs vary between runs.
- Don't reward length; reward usefulness.
- Include a task where the correct answer is "I don't know" to test honesty.
- Re-evaluate periodically; tools change.

### Pitfalls

- Evaluating with a vendor's demo prompts rather than your tasks.
- Ignoring data terms until after purchase.
- Choosing on one lucky output.
- Forgetting the human time needed to fix outputs, which is the real cost.

### Privacy note

Evaluation often tempts people to paste real client material "just to test". Use public or anonymised materials until the tool is approved for your data class.
keyTakeaways: Evaluate on your own tasks using eight criteria: fit, quality, grounding, integration, privacy, cost, reliability and portability.
Run identical prompts and materials across tools and score blind where possible.
Include an 'I don't know' test and repeat important tests; outputs vary.
Only use public or anonymised material until a tool is approved for your data.

lessons.title: Gemini in Google Workspace
lessons.body:
### Two ways to use Gemini

Google's Gemini is available as a standalone assistant (the Gemini app on web and mobile) and as AI built into **Google Workspace** apps such as Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive and Meet. Which features you get depends on whether you use a personal Google account or a Workspace account, your plan, your administrator's settings and your region. Google changes packaging and names regularly, so check the Google Workspace and Gemini help centres for current details.

### What Workspace integration makes possible

The big advantage is **context without copy-paste**. Depending on your setup, Gemini can:

- **Gmail:** summarise long threads, draft replies in context, and help find information across emails.
- **Docs:** draft, rewrite and summarise documents; help create outlines and proposals from your notes.
- **Sheets:** help build formulas, organise data, create tables and explain trends.
- **Slides:** draft slide content and generate images for presentations.
- **Drive:** answer questions across files you have access to, and summarise folders or documents.
- **Meet:** help with note-taking and meeting summaries, where enabled.

Gemini works with content you already have access to; it doesn't grant access to files you couldn't otherwise open.

### Workflow 1: Inbox to action

```text
Summarise this email thread. List:
1. What the client is asking for
2. Deadlines mentioned
3. Open questions we haven't answered
Then draft a reply that confirms the deadline, answers the open questions with [TBC] where I need to fill in details, and proposes a 15-minute call.
```

Review the draft, fill the [TBC] items, and send. You remain the sender and the one accountable.

### Workflow 2: Drive-grounded brief

```text
Using the files "Q3 Campaign Report" and "Brand Guidelines 2026" in my Drive, create a one-page brief for the Q4 campaign:
objective, audience, key messages, what worked in Q3 (with figures from the report), and mandatory brand rules.
Tell me which file each point comes from.
```

Asking which file each point comes from turns a black box into something you can check.

### Workflow 3: Sheets analysis

```text
In this sheet, column B is campaign name, C is spend, D is conversions.
Add a column for cost per conversion, then highlight the three campaigns with the lowest cost per conversion.
Explain the formula you used.
```

Then spot-check two rows by hand.

### Gems: reusable assistants

Gemini offers **Gems**, customised versions of Gemini with your instructions for a recurring task, similar in spirit to custom assistants in other tools. Example: a "Client update writer" Gem with your agency's structure and tone. Availability varies by plan.

### Worked example

An account manager at a UK agency spends Monday mornings catching up on a weekend of client emails. With Gemini in Gmail, she summarises the five longest threads, drafts replies with [TBC] markers, and asks Gemini in Docs to turn the key points into the weekly status report using last week's report as a template. She checks every figure against the source sheet. Her Monday catch-up shrinks from a morning to under an hour, and the report is more consistent.

### Sample output quality check

A good thread summary names who asked what, lists dates exactly as written in the emails, and separates decisions from open questions. If a summary says "the client agreed" without quoting where, ask: "Quote the sentence where the client agreed."

### Admin and privacy considerations

For Workspace accounts, administrators control which Gemini features are enabled. Google publishes commitments about how Workspace data is handled with Gemini for business customers; read the current terms and your organisation's policy. For personal accounts, check activity and data settings in the Gemini app, including whether conversations are saved and reviewed.

### Pitfalls

- Letting AI send or reply on your behalf without review.
- Assuming a summary captured every commitment in a long thread.
- Using a personal Google account for client work.
- Forgetting that shared Drive files may contain other people's confidential information.
keyTakeaways: Gemini is available as a standalone app and inside Google Workspace apps; features vary by account, plan, admin settings and region.
Workspace integration provides context without copy-paste, within your existing permissions.
Ask Gemini which file or email each point comes from, and use [TBC] markers for missing details.
Use Gems for recurring tasks and follow admin and data policies for work accounts.

lessons.title: Gemini's long context and multimodal skills
lessons.body:
### Long context in practice

Gemini models are known for very large **context windows**, meaning they can take in a great deal of material in one go: long reports, many documents, large codebases, lengthy transcripts, and in some cases audio and video. Exact limits depend on the model, the product (app vs API) and your plan, and they change over time.

Long context changes what's practical:

- Ask questions across a **whole folder** of reports rather than one at a time.
- Analyse a **full-length transcript** of a webinar or podcast.
- Compare **several versions** of a policy or contract.
- Review a **long video** for key moments (where video input is supported).

### Multimodal inputs

Gemini is designed to be **multimodal**: it can understand text, images, audio and video, depending on the product. Practical examples:

- **Video:** "Watch this product demo recording and list every feature shown, with timestamps."
- **Audio:** "Summarise this voice note from the client and list the action items."
- **Images:** "Compare these two packaging designs for shelf visibility and readability."
- **Mixed:** "Here's our pitch deck PDF and the recording of the client's feedback call. What objections did they raise and which slides address them?"

### A long-context prompt pattern

```text
I've provided [list of materials].
Task: [question that requires looking across all materials].
Rules:
- Cite the document name and section, or the timestamp for audio/video, for every point.
- If materials disagree, show both versions.
- If something isn't in the materials, say "Not found in materials".
Output: [table / bullet summary / brief].
```

Timestamps are especially valuable for video and audio: they let you jump to the moment and verify.

### NotebookLM: a source-grounded companion

Google also offers **NotebookLM**, a research and note-taking tool built on Gemini that works primarily from the sources you add (documents, websites, videos and more). It is designed to answer with references to your sources, and it can produce study guides and audio overviews. It's a strong choice when you want answers grounded in a defined set of materials, such as a course reading list or a client's document pack. Features vary; check Google's help pages.

### Grounding with search and Deep Research

The Gemini app can use Google Search to ground answers in current information, and offers a **Deep Research** mode that runs multi-step research and produces a cited report, depending on plan and region. Apply the same verification discipline as with any research tool: open sources, check dates, triangulate.

### Worked example

A creator in Lahore records hour-long livestreams. She uploads a recording (where supported) and asks Gemini to identify the five most engaging segments with timestamps and suggest a title and hook for each as a short-form clip. She reviews the timestamps, cuts the clips in her editor, and uses the suggested hooks as first drafts. What used to take an evening of scrubbing through footage now takes much less time.

### Sample output

For the livestream task, a good response returns a table: Timestamp range | What happens | Why it's engaging | Suggested hook. If timestamps are missing or vague ("around the middle"), ask for exact ranges and spot-check the first two.

### Limits and cautions

- **Long isn't the same as thorough.** Models can miss details in very long inputs. Ask targeted questions and check key facts.
- **Upload limits vary.** Large videos or many files may hit product limits.
- **Privacy:** recordings often include other people's voices and faces. Get consent where required and avoid uploading sensitive meetings to non-approved accounts.
- **Rights:** only analyse content you have the right to use.

### Going further

Developers can access Gemini models through Google's AI developer platforms and cloud services, with features for long context, multimodal input and grounding. The same evaluation principles apply: test on your data, measure quality and cost.
keyTakeaways: Gemini's large context windows make it practical to analyse many documents, long transcripts and media in one go.
Multimodal input covers text, images, audio and video, depending on product and plan.
Ask for citations with document names or timestamps, and 'Not found in materials' when absent.
NotebookLM grounds answers in your chosen sources; verify Deep Research outputs like any research.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Timestamps make verification fast and precise.

lessons.title: Microsoft Copilot in Microsoft 365
lessons.body:
### The Copilot family

"Copilot" is Microsoft's brand for AI assistance across its products. For professionals, the key distinction is:

- **Microsoft Copilot (consumer):** a general AI assistant for personal use, available in apps and on the web.
- **Microsoft 365 Copilot (work):** AI built into Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, Teams and other Microsoft 365 apps for organisations, able to work with your work data such as emails, files, chats and meetings, within your permissions.
- **Copilot Chat for work** and **agents**, including options to build custom agents with tools such as Copilot Studio.

Licensing, names and included features change and differ between consumer, business and enterprise plans and by region. Check Microsoft's official documentation and your IT team for what you have.

### What Microsoft 365 Copilot can do in each app

- **Outlook:** summarise threads, draft replies, and help prepare for meetings based on related emails.
- **Teams:** summarise meetings (where recording or transcription is enabled), list action items, and answer "What did I miss?" questions.
- **Word:** draft from prompts and referenced files, rewrite sections, and summarise long documents.
- **Excel:** help create formulas, analyse data, highlight trends and create charts.
- **PowerPoint:** create draft presentations from a prompt or a document and summarise decks.
- **Work chat:** ask questions across your work content, like "What's the latest on the Al Noor account?"

### Workflow 1: Meeting to follow-up

After a Teams meeting with transcription enabled:

```text
Summarise this meeting for people who missed it:
- Decisions made
- Action items with owners and due dates
- Open questions
- Risks raised
Then draft a follow-up email to attendees with the action items as a table.
```

Check owners and dates against your own understanding; transcripts can mishear names and numbers.

### Workflow 2: Document-grounded proposal

```text
Draft a proposal for [client] using /[Past Proposal file] for structure and /[Case Study file] for proof points.
Keep pricing as [TBC]. Use our standard terms section unchanged. Highlight anything you inferred rather than took from the files.
```

In many Microsoft 365 apps, you can reference specific files in prompts; exact syntax varies by app.

### Workflow 3: Excel analysis

```text
Analyse this table of monthly sales by region. Show the top 3 regions by growth rate, create a chart of monthly trends,
and explain any unusual months. Show the formulas used.
```

### Worked example

A sales operations manager in Riyadh receives a 60-minute pipeline review recording and a 200-row Excel export. Copilot in Teams produces the summary and action items; Copilot in Excel identifies deals stuck in the same stage for more than 45 days. She drafts the follow-up email with Copilot in Outlook, adds context only she knows (a client's budget freeze), and sends it. The work that took half a day is done before lunch, and every number was checked against the source spreadsheet.

### Sample output check

A strong meeting summary names owners exactly as they appear in the attendee list, gives dates in a consistent format, and separates "decided" from "discussed". If it says "the team agreed to increase budget" but you remember it as a proposal, correct it before sending; summaries can over-state consensus.

### Etiquette and consent

Tell participants when meetings are recorded or transcribed, follow your organisation's policy and local law, and be cautious with sensitive meetings (HR, legal, medical) where recording may be inappropriate.

### Pitfalls

- Sending AI-drafted emails without reading them.
- Treating a meeting summary as the official record without review.
- Expecting Copilot to know things that aren't in your accessible data.
- Assuming the consumer Copilot app has the same data protections as your work account.
keyTakeaways: Distinguish consumer Copilot from Microsoft 365 Copilot, which works with your work data within your permissions.
Use Copilot across Outlook, Teams, Word, Excel and PowerPoint for summaries, drafts and analysis.
Check owners, dates and numbers in AI meeting summaries; they can mishear or overstate consensus.
Inform participants about recording and transcription and follow policy and law.

knowledgeCheck.question: What most distinguishes Microsoft 365 Copilot from the consumer Copilot app?
options: It works inside Microsoft 365 apps with your organisation's work data, within your permissions
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Microsoft 365 Copilot is grounded in work data and integrated into productivity apps.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Verify names, owners and dates before distributing summaries.

Only the host needs to know

lessons.title: Grounding, permissions and governance for work copilots
lessons.body:
### How work copilots find information

Work copilots such as Microsoft 365 Copilot (and similarly Gemini in Workspace) answer questions by **retrieving** relevant content from your organisation's data (emails, files, chats, calendars) and then generating a response grounded in what they found. In Microsoft's case, this retrieval draws on the organisation's Microsoft 365 data through its underlying services, and it respects existing access permissions: users should only get answers based on content they already have permission to see.

That design has a crucial implication.

### The oversharing problem

If permissions in your organisation are too broad, a copilot can surface information people technically have access to but were never meant to see. For example:

- A salary spreadsheet saved in a folder shared with "Everyone".
- An HR investigation document in a team site with inherited permissions.
- A client's confidential pricing in a widely shared channel.

Before AI, these files were hard to find. With AI, a simple question like "What are the salary bands for managers?" might find them. The AI hasn't broken security; it has exposed weak permissions.

### A readiness checklist for organisations

1. **Audit sharing:** identify sites, folders and files shared with everyone or with large groups, especially those containing sensitive data.
2. **Apply sensitivity labels and data loss prevention** where available, so sensitive content is classified and protected.
3. **Fix inherited permissions** on sensitive sites and archive stale content.
4. **Pilot with a small group** and test prompts designed to find sensitive information ("show me salary data", "contracts with termination clauses") to see what surfaces.
5. **Train users** on responsible prompting and what to do if they see something they shouldn't.
6. **Monitor and review** usage with the admin and compliance tools available on your plan.

### For individual users: responsible habits

- If Copilot shows you something that looks confidential and outside your role, **stop, don't share it, and report it** to IT or your manager.
- Don't use copilots to search for information about colleagues out of curiosity.
- Remember that your prompts and results may be logged for compliance purposes in business environments.
- Verify AI answers against the source documents it references.

### Custom agents and extensions

Organisations can extend copilots with custom agents and connectors to other systems (for example, CRM or ticketing). Each extension widens what the AI can reach. Apply least privilege, test for data exposure, and require approval before agents take actions such as updating records or sending messages.

### Worked example

A 150-person company pilots Microsoft 365 Copilot. During testing, an IT admin asks "What are the bonus amounts for this year?" and Copilot surfaces a spreadsheet from a finance folder that had been shared with a large group years ago. The pilot pauses for two weeks while IT audits sharing on finance and HR sites, applies sensitivity labels, and removes broad access. When the rollout resumes, the same prompt returns nothing sensitive. The AI did the company a favour by revealing a long-standing problem.

### Sample test prompts for a pilot

```text
Show me any documents about salaries, bonuses or compensation.
Summarise any HR investigations or disciplinary cases.
List contracts that mention termination or penalties.
What are our client discount levels?
```

If a pilot user without a legitimate need gets meaningful answers to these, permissions need work.

### The same logic applies elsewhere

Gemini in Workspace, AI features in CRMs, and third-party tools connected via connectors or MCP all rely on the access you grant. Governance is not Microsoft-specific: it's a principle for every embedded AI.

### Pitfalls

- Rolling out work copilots without a permissions review.
- Blaming the AI for exposing data that was already overshared.
- Adding connectors to many systems without assessing what they expose.
keyTakeaways: Work copilots retrieve content from organisational data and respect existing permissions.
Overly broad permissions become visible when AI makes content easy to find: the oversharing problem.
Audit sharing, apply labels and data loss prevention, pilot with sensitive test prompts, and train users.
Every connector or agent widens reach; apply least privilege and approvals.

modules.title: Perplexity and research engines
modules.summary: Use cited answer engines like Perplexity for fast research, and run a repeatable workflow from question to verified brief.

lessons.title: Perplexity: the cited answer engine
lessons.body:
### What makes Perplexity different

**Perplexity** is built around search. Ask a question and it searches the web, reads relevant pages, and writes an answer with **numbered citations** linking to its sources. You can ask follow-up questions that build on the thread. It sits between a traditional search engine (a list of links) and a general assistant (a written answer), with sources front and centre.

Perplexity offers free and paid tiers. Paid tiers typically add more advanced search modes, deeper research features, file uploads, and the option to choose between different underlying AI models. Feature names and inclusions change; check Perplexity's official help centre.

### When an answer engine is the right tool

- **Fact-finding with sources:** "What are the current requirements for [topic] in [country]?"
- **Quick market and competitor scans:** "What products has [company] launched this year?"
- **Explaining news:** "What happened with [event], and what are the different perspectives?"
- **Finding primary sources:** "Link me to the official guidance on [topic]."
- **Pre-meeting research:** "Summarise public information about [company] relevant to a partnership conversation."

For writing long drafts, complex reasoning over your own files, or building tools, a general assistant is often a better fit.

### Asking better questions

Answer engines respond to specificity:

| Weak | Strong |
|---|---|
| influencer rules | Current UK advertising regulator guidance on labelling paid influencer posts, with links to official pages |
| best CRM | CRMs suitable for a 10-person agency in the UAE with WhatsApp integration and Arabic support; compare pricing models |
| AI news | Major announcements about AI regulation in Saudi Arabia in the last 6 months, with official sources |

### Reading citations properly

Citations make verification easier, but they don't make answers automatically correct. Common issues:

- The cited page says something **slightly different** from the summary.
- The source is **outdated** or secondary.
- One claim has **no citation** at all.
- A citation points to a **low-quality** site.

A quick habit: hover over or open the citations for the two or three claims that matter most. If the source doesn't say it, don't use it.

### Workflow: pre-call research in 10 minutes

```text
I have a partnership call with [company] tomorrow. From public sources:
1. What does the company do, and who are its main customers?
2. Recent news (last 12 months): launches, funding, leadership changes, expansions.
3. Any public statements about marketing or creator partnerships.
4. Three smart questions I could ask.
Cite every factual claim.
```

Then open the key sources, note anything surprising, and add your own angle.

### Worked example

A business development manager in Karachi prepares for a call with a regional e-commerce company. Perplexity surfaces a recent expansion announcement and a new leadership hire, with links. She opens the company press release to confirm the expansion and checks the executive's professional profile page. In the call, she references the expansion accurately, which builds credibility. One cited article turned out to be from two years earlier; she ignored it.

### Sample output quality signals

Good: each sentence with a fact has a citation; sources include the company's own site or official registries; dates are given. Weak: vague claims ("the company is growing rapidly") with a single blog citation. When you see weak signals, ask a follow-up: "Find the primary source for the expansion claim."

### Privacy and ethics

- Don't enter confidential client information into public search queries.
- Research companies and public roles, not private individuals' personal lives.
- Respect paywalls and copyright; answer engines summarise, but use original sources properly when you quote.
keyTakeaways: Perplexity is a search-first answer engine that writes answers with numbered citations and supports follow-ups.
Use it for fact-finding, quick scans, news and locating primary sources; use assistants for long drafting and complex reasoning.
Specific questions with scope and source preferences produce better answers.
Citations aid verification but don't guarantee accuracy; open the sources that matter.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Search-first, cited answers are ideal for current, sourced information.

options: Rely on what the source actually says, or find a better source
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The original source is what counts; summaries can distort.

options: CRMs suitable for a 10-person UAE agency with WhatsApp integration and Arabic support, comparing pricing models
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Specific scope and criteria produce targeted, useful answers.

lessons.title: Research workflows: from question to verified brief
lessons.body:
### Research is a process, not a query

Whether you use Perplexity, a general assistant with search, or a deep research mode, good research follows a repeatable process. The tool speeds up each step; it doesn't replace the thinking.

### The five-step research workflow

**1. Frame the question.** Turn a vague topic into answerable questions:

```text
I'm researching [topic] for [purpose/audience]. Help me turn this into 5 specific research questions,
and suggest what types of sources would be authoritative for each (regulator, academic, industry body, company, news).
```

**2. Gather with sources.** Run each question in your answer engine or research mode. For bigger questions, use deeper research modes where available. Save the source links as you go.

**3. Verify.** For each important claim, open the source and classify it:

| Claim | Source | Type (primary/secondary) | Date | Verified? |
|---|---|---|---|---|

Aim for primary sources (regulators, official statistics, company filings, original studies) for anything you'll rely on.

**4. Synthesise.** Paste your verified notes into a general assistant and ask for a structured brief:

```text
Using ONLY the verified notes below, write a 1-page research brief for [audience].
Sections: key findings, implications for us, uncertainties, recommended next steps.
Keep source references in brackets after each point.
```

**5. Review and store.** Have a colleague sanity-check key claims, then store the brief and sources where others can find them (a shared folder, a Project, or a research space).

### Organising ongoing research

Perplexity offers ways to organise research threads and files into collections (for example, **Spaces**), and other tools offer Projects or notebooks. Use them to keep a topic's questions, sources and instructions together, so you don't restart from zero each time. Features vary by plan.

### Choosing sources and focus

Many answer engines let you steer where they search, for example towards academic papers, discussions, or specific sites, and you can always ask for a type of source in the prompt: "Prefer government and regulator sources" or "Include peer-reviewed studies where available." For market data, be wary of numbers from vendors selling into that market; label them.

### Worked example: a student's literature scan

A university student in Manchester needs sources on how AI tools affect small-business marketing. She frames five questions, uses an answer engine with an academic focus to find papers, and opens each in her library portal. Of twelve suggested sources, nine exist and are relevant; three are either tangential or can't be found. She synthesises from the nine verified papers and cites them directly, never citing the AI tool as a source. Her tutor's feedback praises the quality of the references.

### Sample output: a verification log

A short log keeps you honest: "Claim: the regulator requires clear labelling of paid posts. Source: regulator guidance page. Primary. Checked [date]. Verified." "Claim: market grew strongly last year. Source: vendor blog. Secondary, commercial interest. Not independently verified; excluded." Anyone reviewing your brief can see exactly what's solid.

### Red flags that mean "check this now"

- A precise statistic with no citation, or a citation to a page that doesn't contain the number
- A source date more than a year old for fast-moving topics such as regulation, pricing or platform rules
- Every source coming from the same type of site (for example, only vendor blogs)
- Language like "studies show" or "experts agree" with no named study or expert
- A claim that perfectly supports what you hoped to find; confirmation bias is real for humans too

### Comparing tools on the same research question

For important research, run the same question in two tools (for example, an answer engine and a general assistant's research mode). Where they agree and cite primary sources, confidence rises. Where they disagree, you've found exactly the points to check manually.

### Pitfalls

- Citing the AI tool instead of the source.
- Mixing verified and unverified claims in the final brief without labels.
- Over-relying on a single source type.
- Forgetting the date: research reflects what was available when you ran it.
keyTakeaways: Research is a five-step process: frame, gather, verify, synthesise, review and store.
Aim for primary sources and log each claim's source, type, date and verification status.
Synthesise only from verified notes, and never cite the AI tool as the source.
Use research spaces or Projects to keep ongoing topics organised; compare tools on important questions.

knowledgeCheck.question: In a research brief, what should you cite?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Cite the underlying sources, not the tool that found them.

knowledgeCheck.question: Two tools disagree on a key fact. What does that tell you?
options: You've found a point to verify manually against primary sources
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Disagreement highlights where manual verification is needed.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which source type is generally most reliable for a regulatory requirement?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Primary, official sources are most authoritative for regulations.

lessons.activity: Run the five-step workflow on a real question. Produce a one-page brief with a verification log of at least five claims.

modules.title: Open-weight models and local AI
modules.summary: Understand closed vs open-weight models, their licences and trade-offs, and how to run AI privately on your own computer.

lessons.title: Open-weight models explained
lessons.body:
### Closed, open-weight and open source

AI models differ in how they're released:

- **Closed (proprietary) models** are accessed only through the provider's apps and APIs. You never download the model itself. Many of the most capable frontier models are offered this way.
- **Open-weight models** publish the trained model weights so anyone can download and run them, subject to a licence. Well-known families include Meta's **Llama**, **Mistral**'s models, Alibaba's **Qwen**, **DeepSeek**'s models and Google's **Gemma**.
- **Open source** in the strict sense means the weights *and* more of what's needed to understand and reproduce the model (such as code and training details) are released under an open licence. Many "open" models are open-weight but not fully open source, and their licences can include restrictions.

The distinction matters for businesses: **always read the licence**. Some licences permit broad commercial use; others include conditions such as acceptable use policies, attribution, or limits for very large companies.

### Why people use open-weight models

1. **Control:** you choose where the model runs and can customise it.
2. **Privacy:** running on your own hardware or private cloud means data need not leave your environment.
3. **Cost at scale:** for high-volume, well-defined tasks, self-hosting smaller models can be economical, though you pay for hardware and engineering.
4. **Customisation:** fine-tuning on your own data for specialised tasks.
5. **Resilience:** less dependence on a single vendor's pricing or policy changes.

### The trade-offs

- **Capability:** the best open-weight models are strong and improving fast, but the very top hosted models often lead on the hardest reasoning and agentic tasks. This gap changes over time; test for your use case.
- **Effort:** you're responsible for setup, updates, security, monitoring and safety filtering.
- **Hardware:** larger models need powerful GPUs or lots of memory.
- **Safety:** hosted services include safety systems; self-hosted deployments need you to add appropriate safeguards.
- **Licensing and compliance:** you must comply with the licence and applicable laws.

### Model sizes in plain English

Open-weight families usually come in several sizes, described by the number of parameters (for example, "small", "medium" and "large" variants). Rough intuition:

- **Small models** run on laptops and phones; good for simple tasks such as classification, short summaries and drafting.
- **Medium models** need a strong desktop or a single capable GPU; handle many everyday tasks well.
- **Large models** need server-grade hardware or cloud GPUs; approach frontier-level quality on many tasks.

Techniques such as **quantisation** compress models so they run on less memory, with some quality trade-off.

### Worked example: an agency's decision

A digital agency in the UAE processes thousands of customer comments monthly for clients, tagging sentiment and topic. Client contracts require that some data not be sent to external AI providers. The agency tests a medium open-weight model hosted in its own cloud account in-region. After tuning prompts and adding a human review sample, accuracy is acceptable for tagging. For strategy decks and creative work, they continue using a hosted frontier assistant under a business agreement. Result: the right model for each job, with data rules respected.

### Sample decision table

| Need | Hosted frontier model | Open-weight, self-hosted |
|---|---|---|
| Hardest reasoning, long agentic tasks | Usually stronger | Test carefully |
| Strict data residency or offline | Depends on vendor options | Strong fit |
| Low volume, many task types | Simple and cost-effective | Overhead may not pay off |
| High volume, narrow task | Can be costly | Often economical |

### Going further

Open-weight models are available from model hubs and can be served with popular open-source inference tools, or accessed via cloud providers that host them. Evaluate with your own test sets, and document the model version, licence and settings you used.
keyTakeaways: Closed models are accessed via APIs/apps; open-weight models publish weights under a licence; strict open source releases more.
Open-weight models offer control, privacy and customisation at the cost of setup, hardware and safety responsibilities.
Always read the licence; commercial terms and restrictions vary.
Choose per job: hosted frontier models for the hardest tasks, open-weight for control, residency and narrow high-volume work.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does 'open-weight' mean?
options: The model is free of any licence
The trained weights are published for download and use under a licence
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Open-weight models publish weights, typically with licence terms that must be followed.

knowledgeCheck.question: An agency's client forbids sending data to external AI providers. Which option fits best?
options: Run an open-weight model in an environment the agency controls, in line with the contract
Email the data to a friend
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Self-hosted open-weight models can keep data within the agency's environment.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is quantisation?
options: A technique that compresses models to use less memory, with some quality trade-off
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Quantisation reduces model size to run on smaller hardware.

lessons.title: Running AI locally: a practical introduction
lessons.body:
### Why run AI on your own computer?

Running a model locally means the model runs on your laptop or desktop rather than a provider's servers. Reasons people do it:

- **Privacy:** prompts and documents stay on your machine.
- **Offline use:** work without internet, for example while travelling.
- **No per-use cost** after the hardware you already own.
- **Learning:** understand how models behave by experimenting.

It's not for everyone. Local models are usually smaller and less capable than frontier hosted models, and setup takes some effort. But for private notes, simple drafting and experimentation, it can be very useful.

### What you need (conceptually)

- **A reasonably modern computer.** More memory (RAM, or unified memory on some laptops) lets you run larger models. A dedicated GPU helps a lot.
- **A local AI app or runtime.** Popular options include desktop apps with a chat interface and model catalogue, and command-line tools that download and run models. Well-known examples include LM Studio, Ollama and projects built on llama.cpp. Check each tool's official site for supported systems and current features.
- **A model file** sized for your hardware, often a quantised version of an open-weight model.

### A non-engineer's first local session

1. **Choose a desktop app** with a friendly interface from its official website.
2. **Pick a small model** recommended for your hardware (the app often suggests compatible sizes).
3. **Download it** (models can be several gigabytes).
4. **Chat** as you would with any assistant. Try a private task, like summarising your own journal notes or drafting a personal email.
5. **Compare** the result with a hosted assistant on a non-sensitive version of the task to understand the quality gap.

### Good local use cases

- Summarising personal notes and documents you don't want to upload
- Drafting and rewriting short texts
- Classifying or tagging items in bulk
- Offline brainstorming
- Experimenting and learning prompt techniques

Less suitable: complex reasoning, long agentic tasks, up-to-date research (local models don't browse unless you add tools), and tasks that need the very best quality.

### Worked example

A freelance consultant in London keeps sensitive client interview notes. His client agreement prohibits uploading them to third-party services. He runs a medium-sized open-weight model locally to summarise each interview into themes. The summaries are good enough to speed up his analysis; he writes the final report himself, using a hosted assistant only for non-confidential tasks like structuring the report template.

### Sample output expectations

A small local model asked to "summarise these notes into five themes with a supporting quote each" will usually produce a sensible structure but may be less precise: it might merge two themes or pick a weaker quote. Plan a quick human pass. If quality isn't sufficient, try a larger model if your hardware allows, or simplify the task into smaller steps.

### Security and safety notes

- **Download from official sources.** Models and apps from untrusted sites can be malicious.
- **Local doesn't mean automatically secure.** Your laptop's security (encryption, updates, passwords) now protects the data.
- **Safety filtering** may be lighter than in hosted services; use responsibly and within the licence's acceptable use policy.
- **Licences still apply** to local use, particularly for commercial work.

### Going further (technical users)

Local runtimes often expose a local API compatible with common client libraries, so you can connect a local model to scripts, note-taking tools or automation. You can combine a local model with retrieval over your own documents, and compare models with a small evaluation set. Record model version, quantisation level and settings so results are reproducible.

### Pitfalls

- Choosing a model too large for your hardware and concluding "local AI is slow".
- Expecting frontier-level reasoning from a small local model.
- Forgetting to keep apps and models updated.
keyTakeaways: Local AI keeps data on your device and works offline, but models are usually smaller than frontier hosted ones.
You need adequate memory (and ideally a GPU), a local AI app or runtime, and a model sized for your hardware.
Great for private notes, drafting, tagging and learning; less suited to complex reasoning and current research.
Download only from official sources, secure your device, and respect licences.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the main privacy benefit of running a model locally?
options: Prompts and documents can stay on your own device
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Local inference keeps data on your machine.

knowledgeCheck.question: A small local model gives weak answers on a complex analysis. What's the most reasonable response?
options: Try a larger model if hardware allows, simplify the task, or use an approved hosted model for non-sensitive parts
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Match model size and task complexity, and split tasks by sensitivity.

knowledgeCheck.question: Where should you download local AI apps and models from?
options: Official sources and reputable model hubs
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Untrusted downloads can contain malware.

lessons.activity: If your computer allows, install a reputable local AI app, run a small model and compare its answer with a hosted assistant on a non-sensitive task. Note differences in quality and speed.

modules.title: Image, voice and video tools
modules.summary: Choose and use image, voice and video AI tools effectively, with provenance, consent and disclosure built in.

lessons.title: Image generation tools: choosing and using them well
lessons.body:
### The main options

Image generation is now available both in dedicated tools and inside general assistants. Common options include:

- **Midjourney:** known for highly stylised, aesthetic imagery; popular with designers and creators. Accessed via its web app and community platforms, on paid plans.
- **Google's Imagen models:** available in Gemini and other Google products, and to developers via Google's cloud and AI platforms.
- **OpenAI image generation (in ChatGPT and via API):** conversational creation and editing inside an assistant; the DALL·E name has been used for earlier OpenAI image models.
- **Adobe Firefly:** integrated into Adobe's creative apps (for example, generative fill in Photoshop). Adobe positions Firefly as trained on licensed and public-domain content and designed for commercial use; check Adobe's current terms.
- **Open-weight image models** such as the Stable Diffusion and FLUX families, which can be run locally or through various services, subject to their licences.

Capabilities, pricing and terms change often. Check each vendor's official pages, especially commercial-use terms.

### How to choose

| Need | Consider |
|---|---|
| Distinctive artistic style, mood boards | A style-focused dedicated tool |
| Quick visuals while writing or planning | Image generation inside your assistant |
| Editing existing photos inside design workflows | Tools integrated into your design software |
| Enterprise comfort on training data and indemnity | Check vendors' commercial terms and indemnity offers |
| Full control, local generation | Open-weight models with appropriate licences |

### A universal prompt structure

```text
[Subject] + [action/pose] + [setting] + [style/medium] + [lighting] + [composition/camera] + [colour palette] + [mood] + [aspect ratio]
```

Example:

```text
A handmade ceramic mug with Arabic calligraphy pattern on a wooden table beside a window,
product photography, soft morning light, 45-degree angle, shallow depth of field,
earthy neutral palette with teal accents, calm and artisanal mood, 4:5 aspect ratio, no text.
```

Different tools interpret prompts differently; some favour short, keyword-style prompts, others natural sentences. Test and keep a prompt log.

### Iteration and editing

- Change **one variable at a time** (lighting, then composition).
- Use **reference images** where supported to guide style or composition, only with images you have rights to use.
- Use **inpainting/generative fill** to edit parts of an image rather than regenerating everything.
- **Upscale** final choices for print or large formats.

### Worked example

A small candle brand in Birmingham needs seasonal social visuals. The owner generates background scenes (autumn tabletop, cosy window) with an image tool, then composites her **real product photos** into them using her design software's generative fill, so the product is shown accurately. She keeps a prompt log, checks each image for artefacts, and follows her platform's AI-content labelling rules where they apply to realistic edits.

### Sample review checklist

Before using an AI image: Are hands, text, logos and reflections correct? Does the product look like the real product? Are there accidental trademarks or recognisable people? Does the style infringe on a specific living artist's recognisable work? Is labelling or disclosure required on the platform? Would a customer feel misled?

### Provenance and labelling

Industry initiatives such as **Content Credentials** (based on the C2PA standard) attach provenance information to images, and some providers add invisible watermarks (for example, Google's SynthID) to AI-generated content. Platforms increasingly label AI-generated or altered media, and some require you to disclose realistic synthetic content, particularly in ads and sensitive topics. Keep provenance data intact where possible and follow each platform's rules.

### Legal and ethical cautions

- **Copyright and trademarks:** avoid generating recognisable logos, characters or copying specific artworks. Laws on AI-generated works and training data vary by country and are evolving.
- **People:** don't create realistic images of real people without consent; never create deceptive, sexualised or defamatory depictions.
- **Advertising:** images must not mislead consumers about products or results (for example, exaggerated before/after images).
keyTakeaways: Options include style-focused tools, assistant-integrated generators, design-suite tools and open-weight models; terms vary.
Choose by need: style, speed, editing workflow, commercial comfort or local control.
Use a structured prompt, iterate one variable at a time, and composite real products where accuracy matters.
Respect provenance, platform labelling rules, copyright, consent and advertising law.

knowledgeCheck.question: A brand needs social visuals that show its real product accurately. What's the best approach?
options: Generate an AI version of the product
Generate backgrounds with AI and composite real product photos into them
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Compositing real product photos keeps representation accurate.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is Content Credentials (C2PA) about?
options: Attaching provenance information about how content was created or edited
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Content Credentials provide provenance metadata for digital content.

knowledgeCheck.question: When iterating on an AI image, what's the most efficient method?
options: Change one variable at a time and keep a prompt log
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Single-variable changes show what actually improves the image.

lessons.activity: Create three versions of one brand image using the universal prompt structure, changing one variable each time. Run the review checklist on your favourite.

lessons.title: Voice and video AI: ElevenLabs, HeyGen and beyond
lessons.body:
### What voice and video AI can do

A new generation of tools can turn text into natural speech, clone or design voices, dub videos into other languages, and create presenter-style videos with AI avatars. Two widely used examples:

- **ElevenLabs:** known for realistic text-to-speech, voice design and cloning, dubbing into other languages, and audio tools such as sound effects. Available via web app and API.
- **HeyGen:** known for AI avatar videos (a digital presenter speaking your script), creating avatars from your own footage with consent, and video translation with lip-sync.

Other tools offer similar or adjacent capabilities, and general AI platforms increasingly include voice and video generation. Features, languages, pricing and usage rules change; check the official sites.

### High-value use cases

- **Voice-overs** for explainer videos, ads and social content, in several languages.
- **Localisation:** dubbing a founder's video from English into Arabic or Urdu while preserving tone.
- **Training and onboarding videos** with an avatar presenter, easy to update when content changes.
- **Accessibility:** audio versions of articles and course content.
- **Personalised sales videos** at scale (with care; see ethics below).

### A production workflow

1. **Write and approve the script** first. Keep sentences short and conversational; spell out numbers and acronyms the way they should be spoken.
2. **Choose a voice or avatar** you have rights to use: a stock voice or avatar licensed by the platform, or your own cloned voice or avatar created with your explicit consent.
3. **Generate a draft** and listen critically: pronunciation of names, brand terms and local place names; pacing; emphasis.
4. **Adjust** with the tool's controls (speed, stability, pronunciation hints) or by rewriting phrases.
5. **Review with a native speaker** for other languages; automated translation can miss cultural nuance.
6. **Label and disclose** where required by platforms or law.
7. **Store records** of consent, scripts and outputs.

### Script tips for natural speech

```text
Rewrite this script for voice-over:
- Short sentences, one idea each
- Write numbers as spoken ("twenty-five percent")
- Add [pause] where a breath helps
- Keep brand names exactly: [list]
- Target length: 60 seconds at a natural pace
```

### Worked example

An online academy in Lahore records course introductions in English. Using a voice and video translation tool with the instructor's explicit written consent, they produce Urdu and Arabic versions. A native speaker reviews each: two technical terms are mistranslated and corrected in the script before regenerating. Videos are labelled as AI-translated in the description. Enrolment from Arabic-speaking learners grows, and the instructor retains approval rights over every version.

### Consent, ethics and law

This is the most important part of the lesson.

- **Never clone a voice or create an avatar of someone without their explicit, informed consent.** Reputable platforms require consent verification for cloning; don't try to circumvent it.
- **Don't impersonate** real people, public figures or brands. Deepfakes can cause serious harm and may be illegal.
- **Disclose synthetic media** where platforms require it. For example, major video platforms require creators to disclose realistic altered or synthetic content in certain cases; ad platforms have their own rules.
- **Advertising law applies:** an AI presenter giving a "personal testimonial" for a product they never used is misleading.
- **Contracts:** for talent and employees, include clear terms on how their voice and likeness may be used, for how long, and how consent can be withdrawn.
- **Security:** voice cloning is used in scams. Organisations should use call-back verification for payment requests rather than trusting a familiar voice.

### Sample quality checklist

Names pronounced correctly; no robotic emphasis on key words; lip-sync acceptable at normal viewing speed; captions match audio; cultural references appropriate; disclosure present where required; consent documented.

### Pitfalls

- Skipping native-speaker review for translations.
- Using a stock avatar in a way that implies it's a real customer.
- Forgetting to update videos when facts change.
keyTakeaways: Voice and video AI enables voice-overs, dubbing, avatar presenters and accessibility at scale.
Approve scripts first, use licensed or consented voices/avatars, review with native speakers, and keep records.
Never clone voices or likenesses without explicit consent; don't impersonate or mislead.
Follow platform disclosure rules for realistic synthetic media and use verification to defend against voice scams.

knowledgeCheck.question: A client asks you to clone a celebrity's voice for an ad without permission. What should you do?
options: Do it quickly before anyone notices
Decline: cloning a voice without explicit consent is unethical, may be illegal and breaches platform rules
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Consent is essential; impersonation can cause harm and legal liability.

knowledgeCheck.question: What's the most important step when dubbing a video into a language you don't speak?
options: Have a native speaker review the translation and pronunciation
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Native review catches errors and cultural issues.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which practice helps defend a company against voice-cloning scams?
options: Use call-back verification through known channels for payment requests
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Independent verification defeats impersonation attempts.

modules.title: Choosing tools and building your stack
modules.summary: Compare outputs fairly, weigh cost, privacy and lock-in, and design a lean personal AI stack with clear data rules.

lessons.title: Comparing outputs side by side
lessons.body:
### Why compare?

Different AI tools have different strengths, and those strengths shift as models update. Regular side-by-side comparisons on your own tasks are the most reliable way to know which tool to use for what. Module 1 introduced a quick evaluation sprint; this lesson goes deeper into designing fair tests and interpreting results.

### Designing a test set

A good test set is small, representative and reusable:

- **8 to 15 tasks** drawn from real work across your main use cases (writing, analysis, research, planning).
- **A mix of difficulty:** easy, typical and hard.
- **Clear success criteria** for each task, written before you run it: "Must include all 5 deliverables from the brief; under 200 words; no invented figures."
- **At least one honesty test,** where the correct answer is "not enough information".
- **At least one instruction-following test** with several specific constraints.
- **Only non-confidential or anonymised material.**

Save the test set in a document so you can rerun it every few months.

### Scoring that means something

Use a simple rubric for each output:

| Dimension | 1 | 3 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Accuracy | Errors in key facts | Minor errors | No errors found |
| Instruction following | Several constraints missed | One missed | All followed |
| Usefulness | Needs rewrite | Needs edits | Ready with light review |
| Honesty | Invents to fill gaps | Hedges vaguely | Flags gaps clearly |

**Blind scoring** reduces bias: have a colleague paste outputs labelled A and B so you don't know which tool produced which.

### Using one AI to help evaluate another

You can ask an assistant to compare outputs against your criteria:

```text
Here are the task, the success criteria, and two outputs (A and B).
Score each output 1-5 on accuracy, instruction following, usefulness and honesty, quoting evidence from the output for each score.
Then list any factual claims in either output that I should verify manually.
```

This speeds things up, but AI judges have biases (for example, favouring longer answers or their own style). Use AI scoring as a helper, and make final judgements yourself, especially on accuracy.

### Worked example

A content lead at a UK agency compares two assistants on 10 tasks. Results: Tool A wins on long-form writing and following detailed brand rules; Tool B wins on quick research with citations and spreadsheet formulas. Both tie on summaries. Neither passes the honesty test every time. Decision: Tool A as the team's primary writing assistant, Tool B for research tasks, and a new rule that every research claim must be verified by opening the source.

### Sample results summary

A good summary fits on one page: a table of average scores per tool per use case, three notable examples (one strength, one weakness, one surprise for each tool), and a clear recommendation with a re-test date. Keep the raw outputs in an appendix so others can check your judgement.

### Interpreting results wisely

- **Small differences are noise.** Outputs vary between runs; don't switch tools over a one-point difference on a single task.
- **Look at failure modes,** not just averages. A tool that's usually great but occasionally invents figures may be riskier for finance than one that's consistently good.
- **Consider effort-to-fix.** The best output is the one that takes the least human time to make correct and ready.
- **Re-test after major updates.** Rankings change.

### Pitfalls

- Testing with tasks that favour one tool's showcase features.
- Changing the prompt between tools.
- Rewarding confident tone over correctness.
- Treating public benchmark rankings as a substitute for your own tests.
keyTakeaways: Build a reusable test set of 8 to 15 real tasks with success criteria, honesty and instruction-following tests.
Score with a rubric (accuracy, instruction following, usefulness, honesty), blind where possible.
AI can help evaluate, but has biases; make final accuracy judgements yourself.
Focus on failure modes and effort-to-fix, ignore small differences, and re-test after updates.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why write success criteria before running comparison tasks?
options: To judge outputs against a fixed standard rather than being swayed by impressive-looking answers
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Pre-defined criteria reduce bias in evaluation.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is a known bias of using an AI to judge other AI outputs?
options: It may favour longer answers or a style similar to its own
It only scores in odd numbers
knowledgeCheck.explanation: AI judges can have length and style biases; use them as helpers.

knowledgeCheck.question: Tool X scores slightly higher on average but occasionally invents financial figures. For finance reports, what should you consider?
options: The failure mode: occasional invented figures are high-risk for finance work
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Failure modes can matter more than averages for high-stakes tasks.

lessons.title: Cost, privacy and lock-in trade-offs
lessons.body:
### Three questions behind every tool choice

Beyond output quality, three practical questions decide whether a tool belongs in your stack:

1. **What does it really cost?**
2. **Where does my data go, and on what terms?**
3. **How hard would it be to leave?**

### Understanding AI costs

AI tools are priced in a few common ways:

- **Seat subscriptions:** a monthly fee per user, often with usage limits (for example, caps on the most capable models or on deep research runs).
- **Usage-based (API) pricing:** pay per amount of text processed and generated (tokens), with different rates for different models; images, audio and video have their own units.
- **Credits:** common in image, voice and video tools; each generation consumes credits.
- **Bundles:** AI included in broader software licences (office suites, CRMs, design tools), sometimes as add-ons.

To compare fairly, estimate **cost per useful output**, including human time:

```text
Cost per useful output = (tool cost for the period + human time to check and fix x hourly cost) / number of usable outputs
```

A cheaper tool that needs twice the editing may cost more overall.

### Controlling costs

- Audit overlapping subscriptions quarterly; many people pay for three assistants and use one.
- Use faster, lower-cost models for simple, high-volume tasks.
- Set spending limits and alerts on API accounts.
- Check whether tools you already pay for include AI features.
- Choose annual plans only after a successful trial period.

### Privacy: the questions to ask every vendor

1. Is my data used to train models by default? Can I opt out? Does a business plan change this?
2. How long is data retained? Can admins set retention?
3. Where is data processed and stored (data residency)?
4. What security certifications and audits does the vendor have?
5. Is there a data processing agreement for business customers?
6. What admin controls exist (single sign-on, audit logs, user management)?
7. How are connectors and third-party integrations governed?

Match answers against your data classes: public, internal, confidential, restricted. A tool may be fine for public marketing copy but not for client contracts.

### Regional and sector considerations

Organisations in the UK and EU (GDPR), Saudi Arabia (PDPL), the UAE (federal data protection law, plus free-zone regimes in some cases), Pakistan (evolving framework) and US states (various privacy laws) may have obligations on personal data transfers and processors. Regulated sectors (finance, health, government) often have additional rules. Involve your data protection lead; this lesson isn't legal advice.

### Lock-in and portability

Lock-in happens when your workflows, content and knowledge become trapped in one tool. Reduce it by:

- **Keeping prompts, instructions and templates in your own documents,** not only inside a tool.
- **Storing source files in your own drive,** uploading copies to AI tools.
- **Exporting outputs regularly** in standard formats.
- **Preferring open standards** (for example, MCP for connectors) where practical.
- **Avoiding deep dependence on one vendor's unique features** for critical processes unless the benefit clearly outweighs the risk.

### Worked example

A 12-person agency in Jeddah spends on four AI subscriptions per person. An audit shows most staff use one assistant daily and another occasionally. They consolidate to one business-plan assistant for everyone (for data terms and admin controls), a shared research-tool licence for the three strategists, and credits-based image and voice tools for the creative team. Prompts and client instructions move into a shared drive so they're portable. Costs fall, and the data terms improve.

### Sample cost and privacy table

| Tool | Pricing model | Our monthly cost | Training on our data? | Data classes allowed | Export options |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

Fill it in for your current tools; blanks are action items.

### Pitfalls

- Comparing sticker prices without human time.
- Assuming a paid individual plan has business-grade data terms.
- Building critical workflows inside a tool with no export path.
keyTakeaways: Compare cost per useful output, including human time to check and fix.
Control costs by auditing overlaps, matching model tiers to tasks and setting spending limits.
Ask vendors about training use, retention, residency, security, agreements and admin controls.
Reduce lock-in by keeping prompts and files in your own storage and favouring open standards.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Human time often dominates true cost.

options: Keeping all prompts only inside one tool
Storing prompts, instructions and source files in your own documents and exporting outputs
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Portable assets keep switching costs low.

options: Where is data processed and stored?
How many employees does it have?
Does it have a mobile app?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Residency concerns the location of processing and storage.

lessons.title: Building your personal AI stack
lessons.body:
### What a personal AI stack is

Your **AI stack** is the small set of tools you use deliberately, each with a clear job, plus the habits and assets that make them effective. A good stack is **lean** (few tools you know deeply), **fit for purpose** (each tool earns its place), and **safe** (data rules are clear).

### The stack blueprint

Most professionals need something like:

1. **One primary assistant** for writing, analysis and reasoning, on a plan whose data terms match your work.
2. **One research tool** with strong citations (an answer engine or your assistant's research mode).
3. **Your embedded copilot** in the office suite you already use (Workspace or Microsoft 365), if your organisation provides it.
4. **One creative tool** per media type you actually produce (images, voice, video), only if you produce it regularly.
5. **Optional:** a local model for private notes or offline work, and an automation tool for repetitive workflows.

Plus the **assets** that make any tool better:

- A **prompt library** of tested templates
- **Instructions and style guides** you can paste into any tool
- **Reference files** (brand guides, product facts) kept current in your own storage
- A **verification checklist**
- A **data rules card**: what goes where

### Designing your stack in five steps

**Step 1: List your top 10 recurring tasks** and estimate weekly time on each.

**Step 2: Map each task to a category** (assistant, research, embedded copilot, creative, automation).

**Step 3: Choose one tool per category** using your evaluation results and data terms.

**Step 4: Build assets** for your top five tasks: a prompt template, a checklist and reference files.

**Step 5: Review quarterly:** re-test key tasks, cancel unused subscriptions, update assets.

### Example stacks

**Content creator (solo):** primary assistant (scripts, captions, repurposing), research tool (trends, facts), image tool (thumbnails, concepts), voice tool (multilingual voice-overs), scheduler with AI features. Data rules: no brand-partner contracts in consumer tools.

**B2B salesperson:** embedded copilot (email, meetings, CRM notes where provided by employer), primary assistant through the company's business plan (proposals, call prep), answer engine (prospect research). Data rules: customer data only in company-approved tools.

**Agency owner:** business-plan assistant with shared projects per client, research tool for strategists, creative tools for designers, embedded copilot for operations, and a policy covering all of it.

**Student:** primary assistant (study support, feedback on drafts within academic rules), source-grounded notebook tool for readings, reference manager for citations. Rules: follow the institution's AI policy; never submit AI work as your own where prohibited.

### Your data rules card

```text
PUBLIC (published content, general questions): any tool in my stack
INTERNAL (drafts, plans): [primary assistant business plan], [embedded copilot]
CONFIDENTIAL (client data, contracts): [approved tool] only, minimised
RESTRICTED (passwords, payment data, IDs, health data): never in AI tools
```

Print it or pin it where you work.

### Worked example

A freelance marketer in Dubai had seven AI subscriptions and no clear rules. After listing her top 10 tasks, she keeps four tools: a primary assistant on a paid plan with training opt-out configured, an answer engine, an image tool, and a voice tool used monthly on credits. She moves all prompts into a single document organised by task, writes her data rules card, and schedules a quarterly review. She spends less and works faster because she knows each tool deeply.

### Sample quarterly review agenda

1. Re-run five key test tasks on current tools. 2. Check any new features in tools you already pay for. 3. Review spending. 4. Update prompts that underperformed. 5. Check data terms for changes. 6. Decide: keep, replace, or cancel for each tool.

### Pitfalls

- Adding tools without removing any.
- No written data rules.
- Treating the stack as permanent; the landscape changes.
keyTakeaways: A personal AI stack is a lean set of tools with clear jobs, plus reusable assets and data rules.
Typical stack: primary assistant, research tool, embedded copilot, creative tools as needed, optional local/automation.
Design from your top recurring tasks, build assets for the top five, and review quarterly.
A written data rules card makes safe choices quick and consistent.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the best starting point for designing your AI stack?
options: Your top recurring tasks and the time they take
The newest tool on social media
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Stacks should be built around real work.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which asset makes any AI tool more effective and portable?
options: A personal prompt library with tested templates
A screenshot of the pricing page
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Tested prompts transfer across tools and save time.

knowledgeCheck.question: Where should restricted data like passwords and payment details go in your data rules card?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Restricted data should never be entered into AI tools.
